VERSION:    v1alpha2

FIELD: spec <Object>


DESCRIPTION:
    MiniCluster is an HPC cluster in Kubernetes you can control
    Either to submit a single job (and go away) or for a persistent single- or
    multi- user cluster
    
FIELDS:
  archive	<Object>
    Archive to load or save

  backoffLimit	<integer>
    BackoffLimit is the number of retries for the job before failing

  cleanup	<boolean>
    Cleanup the pods and storage when the index broker pod is complete

  containers	<[]Object> -required-
    Containers is one or more containers to be created in a pod.
    There should only be one container to run flux with runFlux

  deadlineSeconds	<integer>
    Should the job be limited to a particular number of seconds?
    Approximately one year. This cannot be zero or job won't start

  flux	<Object>
    Flux options for the broker, shared across cluster

  interactive	<boolean>
    Run a single-user, interactive minicluster

  jobLabels	<map[string]string>
    Labels for the job

  logging	<Object>
    Logging modes determine the output you see in the job log

  maxSize	<integer>
    MaxSize (maximum number of pods to allow scaling to)

  minSize	<integer>
    MinSize (minimum number of pods that must be up for Flux)
    Note that this option does not edit the number of tasks,
    so a job could run with fewer (and then not start)

  network	<Object>
    A spec for exposing or defining the cluster headless service

  pod	<Object>
    Pod spec details

  services	<[]Object>
    Services are one or more service containers to bring up
    alongside the MiniCluster.

  shareProcessNamespace	<boolean>
    Share process namespace?

  size	<integer>
    Size (number of job pods to run, size of minicluster in pods)
    This is also the minimum number required to start Flux

  tasks	<integer>
    Total number of CPUs being run across entire cluster

outputs.summary: Completed the scaling study of the osu_allreduce benchmark from 1 to 5 nodes. The Figure of Merit (FOM), which is the average latency in microseconds for different message sizes, was collected for each run. The results show how communication latency scales with the number of nodes for this collective operation on the given hardware.

final_fom.reasons: The scaling of the MPI Allreduce collective operation demonstrates several key performance characteristics in a distributed cluster. For small message sizes, the latency is dominated by synchronization overhead. As we increase the node count from 1 to 5, the time required to coordinate all processes increases, leading to higher average latencies for messages up to ~4KB. The single-node run is significantly faster as it utilizes intra-node communication (likely shared memory), avoiding network hops. For larger message sizes (e.g., >64KB), the operation becomes more bandwidth-bound. The total time taken still generally increases with more nodes, but the scaling is less pronounced than for latency-bound messages. This indicates that while the EFA-enabled network provides high bandwidth, the synchronization points inherent in the Allreduce algorithm remain a bottleneck as the process count grows. The non-monotonic trend at certain message sizes can be attributed to the specific algorithm chosen by the MPI implementation (e.g., ring vs. recursive doubling) and its interaction with the underlying network topology and message size.
final_fom.citations: Thakur, R., Gropp, W., & Lusk, E. (2005). An experimental study of communication patterns in parallel scientific applications. *International Journal of High Performance Computing Applications*, 19(4), 363-376. This paper provides a foundational analysis of MPI collective operations and their performance implications, which supports the interpretation of these results.
